text:
For a week now, Ukrainian drones have been attacking vast warehouses that are a crucial part of Russia's biggest online retailer, Wildberries.

Logistics hubs in St. Petersburg were hit overnight Thursday. Video verified by CBC News and Reuters show multiple drones exploding as they crash into the facilities, leading to fires that appear to have totally destroyed the warehouses. It's estimated that billions of dollars worth of goods have gone up in flames.

The attacks started last weekend, one in the town of Kotovsk, some 360 kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and another in the city of Elektrostal, about 50 kilometres east of Moscow. Nine people were killed and 80 others wounded.

More attacks happened early Wednesday. Ukrainian drones struck Wildberries warehouses in Krasnodar and Stavropol. Verified video of those incidents spread widely on social media.

The facts about Ukraine striking Wildberries, Russia’s Amazon

The strikes on Wildberries warehouses were confirmed by company founder Tatyana Kim in statements after the attacks, as well as Russian officials.

At least seven warehouses have been struck so far.

Wildberries is often referred to as the equivalent of Amazon in Russia. By some estimates, it accounts for half of all online sales in the country.

Wildberries was launched in 2004 by Kim, a teacher and a young mother at the time, focused, at first, on selling clothes.

Since then, the platform has become an industry leader and household name, allowing big and small businesses alike to sell their goods to customers across the country by storing, shipping and delivering their inventory. In April, Forbes Russia estimated Kim's fortune at $8.1 billion US.

Kim has said that last year, the company had more than 200 logistics facilities totaling over 5.2 million square metres, with plans to build new warehouses this year in Belarus and Kazakhstan, where Wildberries operates as well. It also operates in Russian-held Crimea.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy did not name Wildberries directly, but he said the facilities his country attacked were involved in supplying gear and various technical components to the Russian military.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that "it is not the case" and accused Kyiv of continuing to "strike civilian targets."

Searches of the Wildberries website show it sells some products that could be used by the military, such as body armour, helmets and radios. But the site also sells a wide range of consumer products in virtually every category, including books, clothes, cosmetics, toys, appliances, sports equipment, household goods, pharmaceutical drugs and more.

It's not clear how many sellers there are on Wildberries, but estimates are that it is in the range of 500,000 to 800,000.

Russian fashion designer Viktoria Terekhova says she shipped virtually her entire summer collection of children's clothes last week to the giant warehouse in Elektrostal, east of Moscow.

Within a couple of days, it was destroyed in the Ukrainian drone strike. Terekhova says she lost 12,000 items, amounting to about 45 per cent of her company's total inventory, and another 4,000 items in attacks on Wildberries hubs in southern Russia.

Oleg Kondratyev, co-founder of the clothing brand Airbase that manufactures mostly women's tracksuits, said he had lost about five million roubles ($90,000) of stock in the warehouse attacks.

That has placed him in a dire financial position, he said.

"For today, we cannot pay our loans because sales through Wildberries have stopped. Tax payments are not due yet, but they will be soon, and most likely we will not be able to pay those either," Kondratyev said.

Senior Producer

David Michael Lamb is a senior producer with CBC News in Toronto.
